e.etymology: Probably a fanciful spelling of Malia, the Hawaiian form of Maria (Mary), with the -iyah ending of Aaliyah. It peaked in 2009, the year Malia Obama's family moved into the White House.

e.meaning: noble (Sanskrit arya); also a spelling of Aria, melody
e.etymology: A spelling that overlaps two names: Arya, a Sanskrit and Persian name meaning noble, and Aria, the Italian word for an operatic solo.

assoc.t: Nissan Ariya electric SUV
Arya Stark of Game of Thrones (similar sound)

e.etymology: A Latinized form of Germanic names beginning with amal, vigor or work, such as Amalberga. Amelia is its better-known English offshoot.

From Greek myth, where Atreus is a king of Mycenae and the father of Agamemnon and Menelaus. The name is usually read as fearless. Its recent rise follows the son of Kratos in the 2018 video game God of War.

assoc.t: son of Kratos in the God of War video games
king of Mycenae in Greek myth, father of Agamemnon

e.note: In Greek myth Atreus kills his brother's sons and serves them at a feast, and his family line is cursed.

e.etymology: An Anglicized spelling of Ciara, the feminine of Ciaran, from Irish ciar, dark or black. Actress Keira Knightley made this spelling familiar in the 2000s.
namesakes: Keira Knightley (actress, Pirates of the Caribbean)

assoc.t: Keira Knightley, British actress

e.etymology: A common spelling of Muhammad, from the Arabic root h-m-d, to praise. It is the name of the prophet of Islam and, across its spellings, one of the most widely given names in the world.
namesakes: Mohamed Salah (Egyptian soccer star)

assoc.t: the prophet of Islam, usually spelled Muhammad

e.etymology: A modern American name that extends Jamar, or joins the popular Ja- prefix to Amari.
From the Spanish word alondra, lark. The 1995 Mexican telenovela Alondra helped spread it among Spanish-speaking families in the US.
A spelling of Elowen, a modern Cornish name taken from the Cornish word for elm tree. The -wyn ending echoes Welsh names such as Bronwyn.

From Latin Beatrix, she who makes happy, perhaps reshaped from Viatrix, traveler. Dante's guide through Paradise and the sharp-witted heroine of Shakespeare's Much Ado About Nothing both carry the name.
namesakes: Princess Beatrice (granddaughter of Queen Elizabeth II)
Beatrice Prior (heroine of the Divergent series)
Beatrice Portinari (Dante's muse in the Divine Comedy)

assoc.t: Beatrice, heroine of Much Ado About Nothing
Beatrice, Dante's guide through Paradise

e.etymology: From Hebrew Shimshon, probably from shemesh, sun. In the Book of Judges, Samson is the strongman whose power lay in his uncut hair until Delilah betrayed him.

assoc.t: biblical strongman of Samson and Delilah

e.etymology: The Italian form of Alexander, from Greek Alexandros, built from alexein, to defend, and aner, man.
namesakes: Alessandro Volta (inventor of the electric battery)

e.etymology: A spelling of Dominic, from Late Latin Dominicus, of the Lord. It honors Saint Dominic, the Spanish priest who founded the Dominican order.

Popularized by Dax (Diogenes Alejandro Xenos), the hero of Harold Robbins's 1966 novel The Adventurers and its 1970 film. It also matches Dax, a spa town in southwestern France, and doubles as a short form of Daxton.
namesakes: Dax Shepard (actor and podcast host)

assoc.t: Dax Shepard, actor and podcast host
Jadzia Dax of Star Trek: Deep Space Nine
spa town in southwestern France

e.meaning: feminine form of Brian, perhaps high or noble
e.etymology: A feminine form of the Irish name Brian, whose Celtic root may mean high or noble. Edmund Spenser used Briana in The Faerie Queene, and it came into regular use in the 1970s.

e.meaning: Spanish phonetic form of Diana, the Roman moon goddess
e.etymology: A Spanish spelling that captures the English pronunciation of Diana, the Roman goddess of the hunt and the moon. Paul Anka's 1957 song Diana may have helped spread it in Latin America.
From Cassius, the name of an old Roman family. Gaius Cassius Longinus led the plot against Julius Caesar, and boxer Muhammad Ali was born Cassius Clay.
namesakes: Cassius Clay (birth name of boxer Muhammad Ali)
Cassius (conspirator in Shakespeare's Julius Caesar)

assoc.t: Cassius Clay, birth name of boxer Muhammad Ali

e.etymology: The Spanish form of Henry, from Old High German Haimirich, built from heim, home, and rihhi, ruler.
namesakes: Enrique Iglesias (Spanish pop singer)
e.note: The traditional Spanish nickname Kike (KEE-keh) is spelled like an anti-Jewish slur in English.

assoc.t: Enrique Iglesias, Latin pop singer

e.meaning: pet form of Katherine, long linked to Greek katharos, pure
e.etymology: A pet form of Katherine and Kate that is often given on its own. Katherine comes from Greek Aikaterine, whose origin is debated; it was linked early on to katharos, pure.
namesakes: Katie Holmes (actress)
Katie Couric (TV journalist)
Katie Ledecky (Olympic swimming champion)

e.meaning: pet form of Os- names such as Oscar and Oswald
e.etymology: A pet form of names beginning with Os-, such as Oscar, Oswald and Osborne. Rock singer Ozzy Osbourne, born John Osbourne, got it from his surname.
namesakes: Ozzy Osbourne (Black Sabbath singer and reality TV star)

assoc.t: Black Sabbath frontman Ozzy Osbourne

e.etymology: The Spanish and Portuguese form of Moses, from Hebrew Moshe. Exodus ties the name to a Hebrew verb for drawing out of water; many scholars trace it to an Egyptian word for child.
namesakes: Moises Alou (All-Star outfielder)

e.etymology: A respelling of Avery, an English surname that grew from the Norman French form of Alfred, Old English for elf counsel.
From Scottish Gaelic ruadh, red or red-haired, as in the outlaw Rob Roy. It was also read as Anglo-Norman roy, king, which added to its appeal.
namesakes: Roy Rogers (singing cowboy film star)
Roy Orbison (singer of Oh, Pretty Woman)
Roy Kent (gruff footballer in Ted Lasso)

e.meaning: short form of Mackenzie, child of Coinneach
e.etymology: A short form of Mackenzie, from the Scottish surname MacCoinnich, son of Coinneach (Kenneth). It has been given as a name in its own right since the 2000s.

e.meaning: from a Germanic name ending in ric, ruler
e.etymology: A modern spelling of Emery, an English surname from the Norman name Aimeri or Emmerich, a Germanic compound whose second element ric means ruler.

e.meaning: feminine form of Max, from Latin maximus, greatest
e.etymology: An English feminine form of Max, coined in the late 1800s with the fashionable -ine ending. Max comes from Latin maximus, greatest. Stage actress Maxine Elliott spread it in the 1890s.
namesakes: Maxine Waters (longtime California congresswoman)

assoc.t: Maxine, the cranky Hallmark greeting-card character

e.etymology: From Hebrew Sha'ul, asked for. Saul was the first king of Israel, and Saul of Tarsus was the original name of the apostle Paul.
namesakes: Saul Bellow (Nobel Prize-winning novelist)
King Saul (first king of Israel in the Bible)

assoc.t: lawyer Saul Goodman of Better Call Saul

e.etymology: From the Spanish word sierra, a jagged mountain range, literally a saw, as in the Sierra Nevada. It became an American girls' name in the 1980s and 1990s.

assoc.t: Sierra Nevada mountains of California
GMC Sierra pickup truck
the letter S in the NATO phonetic alphabet
Sierra, off-price outdoor gear retailer

e.etymology: From Hebrew Zekharyah, Yahweh has remembered, shaped by the Greek and Latin form Zacharias. It is the fuller form of Zachary and a variant of the prophet's name Zechariah.
A variant of Alan, a Celtic name that Bretons brought to England after the Norman Conquest; its meaning is uncertain. As a first name, Allen is often taken from the surname.
namesakes: Allen Iverson (Hall of Fame NBA guard)
Allen Ginsberg (Beat poet, author of Howl)

assoc.t: Allen wrench, the L-shaped hex key

e.etymology: An Anglicized form of Sean as pronounced in Ulster, which makes it an Irish form of John, from Hebrew Yochanan, God is gracious. The 1953 Western Shane spread it in the US.

assoc.t: Shane, the classic 1953 Western film

e.etymology: The Greek and Latin form of Jonah, from Hebrew Yonah, dove. In Lithuanian the same spelling is the form of John.
namesakes: Jonas Salk (developer of the polio vaccine)
Jonas (hero of Lois Lowry's The Giver)

assoc.t: Jonas Brothers, the sibling pop band
